vignette:
The stage manager's voice had been calm over the house intercom that night, two years ago, telling everyone to stay seated. Maya had been in the wings, waiting for her cue, when the gunfire started in the orchestra pit. She never saw the shooter-only heard the pops, the screaming, the thud of bodies hitting the floor. She crouched behind a stack of set pieces, her hands over her ears, her breath coming in ragged gasps. When it was over, she walked out past a police officer who was shouting into a radio, his rifle still raised. She couldn't put the event into words afterward; when she tried to tell her therapist what she had seen, the memory came in disconnected pieces-the smell of cordite, the flash of a uniform sleeve, the sound of someone sobbing. She couldn't find a story to hold it together.

In the months that followed, Maya began to feel like an outsider, even among her fellow actors who had been there. She was certain that the people responsible had faced no consequences-the shooter had been killed on scene, and there had been no trial, no accountability, no closure. This sense of injustice hardened into a belief that she was permanently set apart from others, that no one could understand what she carried. She became convinced that danger was everywhere. Even when friends told her the theater was safe, she found it impossible to believe them. She started choosing her seat on the subway based on where she felt most protected-back against a wall, exit in sight-and she began avoiding public transport altogether when she could afford it. The isolation deepened. She felt isolated and set apart from others, and her spending spiraled: she bought expensive clothes and electronics she didn't need, using the rush of a purchase to distract herself from the fear that lived in her chest.

The memory of that night would surge up without warning. When she saw a police officer on the street, or a military uniform in a film, she felt the event happening right now-the sound of the pops, the weight of the set piece against her back. These reliving episodes terrified her, and they reinforced her belief that she could not trust her own safety. The more she felt the memory as present and real, the more she scanned every room for exits and threats. And the more she scanned, the more the memory intruded, as if her vigilance were a magnet pulling the fragments back into view. She had come to believe that her hypervigilance was the only thing keeping her alive, even as it exhausted her.

Her work suffered. She turned down roles that required her to be near any prop that resembled a weapon, and she stopped auditioning for plays set in police stations or military contexts. She told her agent she was only available for contemporary domestic dramas, but even those felt unsafe when the stage lights dimmed and the audience went quiet. The compulsive spending became a way to manage the dread: a new handbag, a pair of boots, anything to interrupt the loop of memory and threat. But afterward, she felt more isolated than before-she had spent money she didn't have, and she had nothing to show for it but a closet full of things that reminded her of her own desperation.

Last week, she saw a police officer standing outside her apartment building, and she fled back inside, her heart hammering. She realized she could not keep living this way-avoiding her neighborhood, her profession, her own mind. She came to therapy because she was terrified that the fear would never stop, and because she was hoping, against all evidence, that someone could help her find a way back to the person she had been before the shots rang out.
